title: The twelve pitch classes
description: Drill the twelve classes, accidentals, enharmonics, and the one-string chromatic layout.

cards.front: What are the seven natural pitch classes?
cards.back: A B C D E F G.

cards.front: Why are there twelve pitch classes?
cards.back: The octave is split into twelve equal steps (twelve-tone equal temperament). Seven letters name the diatonic naturals; accidentals name the other five.

cards.front: Why do only five of the twelve classes need accidentals?
cards.back: B–C and E–F have no class between them. The other five neighboring natural pairs each have one in-between class. 7 + 5 = 12.

cards.front: What does a sharp do? What does a flat do?
cards.back: A sharp (♯) raises a note by one half step (one fret). A flat (♭) lowers a note by one half step.

cards.front: What does enharmonic mean? Give one pair.
cards.back: Two names for the same pitch class. Example: C♯ and D♭ — same fret, different spelling.

cards.front: Which neighboring naturals have no pitch class between them?
cards.back: B to C, and E to F.

cards.front: Which natural pairs have one class between them?
cards.back: C–D, D–E, F–G, G–A, and A–B.

cards.front: List the twelve pitch classes from C, showing both names where they exist.
What comes after B in the chromatic cycle?
cards.back: C again, one octave higher. The twelve-class cycle repeats.

cards.front: List the twelve classes starting from A, using sharps.
cards.back: A A♯ B C C♯ D D♯ E F F♯ G G♯.

cards.front: List the twelve classes starting from A, using flats.
cards.back: A B♭ B C D♭ D E♭ E F G♭ G A♭.

cards.front: Give an enharmonic name for G♯, E♭, F♯, B♭, and D♯.
What are E♯, F♭, B♯, and C♭ as everyday names?
cards.back: E♯ = F, F♭ = E, B♯ = C, C♭ = B. Double sharps and double flats also exist.

cards.front: When is C♯ the right spelling, and when must it be D♭?
cards.back: It depends on context: the key, the chord, and the interval you are naming. Same guitar fret, different harmonic role.

cards.front: Is “sharps going up, flats going down” a law of spelling?
cards.back: No. It is a common convention for writing a chromatic run, not a rule of theory.

cards.front: On string 6, name frets 0 through 12 starting from open E (sharps).
cards.back: E F F♯ G G♯ A A♯ B C C♯ D D♯ E.

cards.front: On string 5, name frets 0 through 12 starting from open A (sharps).
cards.back: A A♯ B C C♯ D D♯ E F F♯ G G♯ A.

cards.front: Where can you see the E–F and B–C half steps on the neck?
cards.back: E–F: string 6 frets 0–1. B–C: string 6 frets 7–8, and string 5 frets 2–3.

cards.front: What happens twelve frets above any note on one string?
cards.back: You land on the same pitch class one octave higher. Frets 0–12 show each class at least once per string.

cards.front: What pitch class is 7 half steps above D? 5 above B? 3 below C?
cards.back: A, E, and A.

cards.front: Seven classes above E is which class? Three below A?
cards.back: Seven above E is B. Three below A is F♯.

cards.front: On a fretted guitar in equal temperament, can you hear C♯ as different from D♭?
cards.back: No. They are the same fret and the same sound. Notation still needs the right spelling for the harmonic role.
